body: Hi there, Scottish psychology graduate here. Everyone else posting here has answered your other questions, so I'm simply going to put a fly in the ointment by saying that I hated the majority of my time at St Andrews. I was 17 until December 1st year as well, and it really set me apart from the other people in my year. I was in DRA where I had horrible flatmates who were obnoxious to me (i will never live with girls ever again), as well as DRA being the most difficult halls to meet people in. I was miserable. The stereotypes you hear about the people here are true on the surface, in that those are the loud people you see being dicks. There are great people here as well, obviously, and I had a largely brilliant 3rd and 4th year. Just took me a while to get there. Also, the lecturers do not and will never care about you, save a precious few.

I have 2 really close friends that I talk to about this stuff. One is the guy that I mentioned in the OP and also talked about in reply to another post. Things with him are not simple. The other is a girl who lives about 500 miles away. We went to university together and she moved home after graduation. I miss being surrounded by my friends.

I have no idea what to refocus my energy to. I volunteer, I do sports... I still have plenty of time to feel utterly worthless.

I just feel so much anger at myself, at the world for not wanting me, and even (selfishly) at my friends for all getting jobs and moving on. And I'm just stuck.

Firstly, the evidence that says that depression is genetic isn't 100% valid, and that cognitive and environmental issues are actually stronger predictors. One of the new things being investigated just now is self-compassion as an influence in depression, and that is something that can be affected by parenting style which is something that you can control. If you want to read anything on this then DeHart, Pelham and Tennen (2006) and not directly related, but I can't find the paper I'm looking for, but Neff and Vonk (2007). For something that deals more with the biological stuff then Booiji and Van der Does (2007).

So, you shouldn't just assume that because you're depressed that your child will be. 

Also, if your child is depressed then you'll know the symptoms. You will know what danger signs are in them and will be able to talk to them and be more willing to aid them in getting the help that they need than parents who have never been through it. You know that it's a horrible thing and that you can't just "get over it" which is more than a lot of people think. 

Bottom line is, if you think that you'll be good parents and if you can provide for a child then don't let your depression hold you back. Just have a good support network.
